issues.legal_issue: Specific performance may be refused when the circumstances make enforcement inequitable and performance would cause greater unforeseen hardship to the defendant than non-performance would cause to the plaintiff.
material_facts: The agreement depended on obtaining several governmental permissions and sanctions, which the purchaser was expected to secure but did not secure within a reasonable time.
Part of the property was subject to legal restrictions on transfer, part was acquired, and the proposed multi-storeyed development appeared impracticable.
The seller remained in possession of most of the property, while the purchaser had possession of only a small part.
The property's value had risen substantially after the agreement, and the purchaser did not show that its conduct made refusal of specific performance inequitable.
issues.conclusion: The court refused to decree specific performance because, considering the circumstances as a whole, enforcement would cause the seller unforeseen hardship without comparable hardship to the purchaser.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary; the discretion must be exercised judicially on sound principles and is subject to appellate correction. Comparative hardship may justify refusal, although mere inadequacy of consideration or an onerous bargain does not by itself establish unfair advantage or unforeseen hardship. The court relied on Lourdu Mari David v. Louis Chinnaya Arogiaswamy, Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, and K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan, including the principle that the court must consider surrounding circumstances and specified time limits, particularly for urban immovable property.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and purchaser_failed_to_perform_within_reasonable_time and (required_approvals_unavailable or subject_property_partly_untransferable or planned_development_impracticable) and unforeseen_hardship_to_seller_exceeds_hardship_to_purchaser and purchaser_did_not_show_inequity_in_refusal

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A party sought a decree compelling performance of an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.purchaser_failed_to_perform_within_reaso: The purchaser did not carry out the obligations needed to complete the transaction within a reasonable time.
predicates.required_approvals_unavailable: Permissions or sanctions needed to carry out the transaction were not obtained.
predicates.subject_property_partly_untransferable: Some of the property covered by the agreement could not be transferred.
predicates.planned_development_impracticable: The proposed development of the property appeared impracticable.
predicates.unforeseen_hardship_to_seller_exceeds_ha: Enforcing the agreement would cause the seller unforeseen hardship greater than the hardship non-enforcement would cause the purchaser.
predicates.purchaser_did_not_show_inequity_in_refus: The purchaser did not establish that its conduct or reliance made it inequitable to refuse specific performance.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance claim follows unreasonable non-performance and significant obstacles, the court may refuse enforcement if the resulting unforeseen hardship to the seller outweighs the hardship to the purchaser and refusal is not shown to be inequitable.

issues.legal_issue: Even when time is not expressly made essential to a contract for the sale of immovable property, the parties must perform within a reasonable time assessed in light of the agreement and surrounding circumstances.
material_facts: The agreement did not state a fixed deadline for performance, but contemplated that plans and clearances would be obtained and construction completed within a period that indicated an expectation of performance within a few years.
The purchaser was responsible for securing the necessary approvals and clearances.
The transaction remained incomplete for several years before litigation began.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser's delay in performing its obligations was not reasonable, notwithstanding the absence of an express fixed deadline for completing the agreement.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the court's discretion must be exercised with regard to the agreement's time limits and all relevant circumstances. Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani establishes that time is not presumed to be of the essence in sales of immovable property, but reasonable time may be inferred from the agreement, the property, and surrounding circumstances. K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan holds that contractual time limits cannot be ignored and that reasonable time must be assessed in context.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and immovable_property_sale_contract and contract_does_not_expressly_make_time_essential and agreement_indicates_expected_timing_for_performance and purchaser_delayed_beyond_reasonable_time_in_context

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A party sought a decree compelling performance of an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.immovable_property_sale_contract: The agreement concerned the sale or transfer of immovable property.
predicates.contract_does_not_expressly_make_time_es: The agreement did not expressly provide that time was essential to performance.
predicates.agreement_indicates_expected_timing_for_: The agreement's terms indicated when particular steps or performance were expected.
predicates.purchaser_delayed_beyond_reasonable_time: The purchaser did not perform within a reasonable time assessed in light of the agreement and surrounding circumstances.

issues.definition: For an immovable-property sale in which time is not expressly essential, a purchaser is in default when the agreement indicates expected timing and the purchaser delays beyond what is reasonable in context.

issues.legal_issue: A contract that has become frustrated because required permissions were unavailable and performance was legally or practically obstructed is not revived merely because a later legal change removes one obstacle.
material_facts: The proposed transfer and development required permissions that were repeatedly not obtained.
For an extended period, part of the property could not be transferred because of restrictions on excess land, and part of the property was acquired.
The relevant restrictions were later repealed, but the court found that the contract had already stood frustrated and declined to use the later repeal to revive it.
issues.conclusion: The contract had stood frustrated under Section 56 of the Contract Act, 1872, and the later repeal of the land restriction did not revive it for specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 56 of the Contract Act, 1872 applies where a contract becomes impossible or unlawful to perform. The court held that the contract had stood frustrated in the circumstances and that subsequent events could not be used to revive it so as to decree specific performance.

rule.if: property_transfer_or_development_contract and required_permissions_repeatedly_unavailable and (legal_restriction_prevented_transfer or part_of_property_was_acquired) and contract_had_become_unperformable_before_later_legal_change and later_legal_change_removed_an_obstacle

predicates.property_transfer_or_development_contrac: The contract concerned transferring property or carrying out development on it.
predicates.required_permissions_repeatedly_unavaila: Permissions required to carry out the contract were repeatedly not obtained.
predicates.legal_restriction_prevented_transfer: A legal restriction prevented transfer of some of the property.
predicates.part_of_property_was_acquired: The state acquired part of the property covered by the contract.
predicates.contract_had_become_unperformable_before: The contract had become unperformable before a later legal change occurred.
predicates.later_legal_change_removed_an_obstacle: A later legal change removed at least one obstacle to performance.

issues.definition: A later legal change does not revive a property contract that had already become unperformable because permissions were unavailable and legal or acquisition obstacles intervened.

issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff cannot obtain specific performance of a contract subject to a variation unless the variation falls within a recognized statutory ground.
material_facts: Part of the property covered by the agreement had become unavailable for transfer.
The purchaser offered to accept the remaining transferable property without a corresponding reduction in the agreed price.
The court found that the circumstances did not involve fraud, mistake of fact, misrepresentation, failure to produce an intended legal result, or a subsequent variation by the parties.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser could not obtain specific performance of the agreement as varied to cover only the property that remained available for transfer.
issues.legal_principle: Section 18 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits enforcement subject to a variation set up by the defendant only in the specified circumstances: fraud, mistake of fact, misrepresentation, failure of the contract to produce an intended legal result, or a subsequent variation of its terms. The court held that none applied.

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A party sought a decree compelling performance of an agreement.
predicates.requested_performance_varies_the_contrac: The requested performance would change the terms or subject matter of the agreement.
predicates.part_of_contract_subject_matter_unavaila: Some of the subject matter covered by the agreement was no longer available for transfer or performance.
predicates.none_of_recognized_variation_grounds_app: The circumstances did not include a recognized ground for enforcing the contract subject to a variation.

issues.definition: When requested performance changes an agreement whose subject matter is partly unavailable, enforcement subject to that change is unavailable if no recognized ground for variation applies.

issues.legal_issue: A court may award compensation in substitution for specific performance even when the contract has become incapable of specific performance.
material_facts: The purchaser claimed compensation as an alternative or additional remedy in its suit.
The court refused specific performance and found the contract incapable of precise performance in the circumstances.
The court considered compensation appropriate and awarded it in substitution for specific performance.
issues.conclusion: The court awarded compensation in substitution for specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 authorizes compensation in addition to or in substitution for specific performance. Its explanation makes clear that a contract's incapacity for specific performance does not preclude the court from awarding compensation.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and contract_incapable_of_specific_performance and compensation_claimed and court_finds_compensation_appropriate

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A party sought a decree compelling performance of a contract.
predicates.contract_incapable_of_specific_performan: The contract could not be specifically performed in the circumstances.
predicates.compensation_claimed: The claimant sought compensation in the proceedings.
predicates.court_finds_compensation_appropriate: The court determined that compensation should be awarded in the circumstances.

issues.definition: When specific performance is sought but the contract cannot be specifically performed, a court may award compensation in substitution if compensation was claimed and is found appropriate.
